concepts.name: Constitutional Grounds for Disqualification under Article 102
key_dimensions: Exhaustive list of disqualification grounds: office of profit, unsound mind, insolvency, non-citizenship, law-made disqualifications
Distinction between disqualification at time of election vs. after becoming a member
UPSC trap: Article 102 applies to both Lok Sabha and Rajya Sabha members equally
Difference between disqualification (Art. 102) and vacation of seat (Art. 101)

concepts.name: Office of Profit Disqualification: Scope and Exemptions
key_dimensions: Constitutional definition vacuum — Parliament defines 'office of profit' via legislation (Parliament (Prevention of Disqualification) Act, 1959)
Three-pronged judicial test: appointment by government, payment by government, removal by government
Exempted offices notified by Parliament and State Legislatures — UPSC trap on who can exempt
Recent controversies: Jaya Bachchan case (2006) — SC ruling on 'office of profit' scope

concepts.name: President's Role in MP Disqualification (Article 103)
key_dimensions: President decides on disqualification questions under Art. 102(1) — except anti-defection cases
Mandatory consultation with Election Commission — President bound by EC's opinion (post-1992 judicial interpretation)
UPSC trap: President acts on EC's advice, NOT the Council of Ministers' advice in disqualification matters
Distinction from State Legislature disqualification — Governor refers to EC, same binding opinion rule

concepts.name: Anti-Defection Law: Tenth Schedule — Core Provisions
key_dimensions: Added by 52nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1985 — grounds for disqualification: voluntary giving up membership, voting contrary to party direction, abstention
UPSC trap: 'Voluntarily giving up membership' ≠ formal resignation — SC held conduct can imply voluntary giving up (Ravi Naik case)
Original provision for merger (1/3rd split) replaced by 2/3rd merger requirement via 91st Amendment, 2003
Speaker/Chairman as deciding authority — not the President/Governor

concepts.name: Tenth Schedule: Exemptions and the Merger Exception
key_dimensions: Two surviving exemptions post-91st Amendment: Speaker election vote, merger (2/3rd members agreeing)
Original third exemption (split) abolished by 91st Amendment, 2003 — UPSC frequently tests this change
Merger must be with another political party — merging faction cannot simply form a separate group
UPSC trap: Individual MPs cannot claim merger exemption; minimum 2/3rd of original party's legislative strength required

concepts.name: Speaker/Chairman as Tribunal under Tenth Schedule: Powers and Judicial Review
key_dimensions: Speaker acts as a tribunal — final authority on disqualification under Tenth Schedule
Kihoto Hollohan case (1992): SC upheld Tenth Schedule validity but ruled Speaker's decision subject to judicial review on grounds of malafides, perversity, violation of natural justice
UPSC trap: Speaker's decision is NOT final and immune — it can be reviewed by High Courts and Supreme Court
Controversy: Speaker belonging to ruling party creating conflict of interest — Law Commission recommended independent tribunal

concepts.name: Timeframe for Deciding Disqualification Petitions: Judicial Interventions
key_dimensions: No constitutional time limit prescribed for Speaker to decide disqualification petitions
Rajendra Singh Rana case (2007): SC held that inordinate delay by Speaker is subject to judicial intervention
Keisham Meghachandra Singh case (2020): SC directed Speaker to decide within a reasonable time — suggested 3-month norm
UPSC trap: Despite SC directions, no statutory time limit exists — remains a constitutional gap

concepts.name: Disqualification on Ground of Insolvency and Unsound Mind
key_dimensions: Adjudged insolvent — disqualification continues until discharged by court; UPSC trap: discharge ends disqualification
Unsound mind — must be declared so by a competent court; self-declaration insufficient
These disqualifications are self-operating — no reference to President/EC needed
Distinction: These are personal incapacity grounds vs. office of profit (external relationship grounds)

concepts.name: Disqualification for Citizenship: Article 102(1)(d)
key_dimensions: Disqualified if not a citizen of India, or has voluntarily acquired citizenship of a foreign state, or is under acknowledgment of allegiance to a foreign state
UPSC trap: Dual citizenship holders are disqualified — India does not permit dual citizenship for parliamentary membership
Overseas Citizenship of India (OCI) holders cannot contest elections — confusion with NRI voting rights
Voluntary acquisition vs. involuntary acquisition distinction — only voluntary acquisition triggers disqualification

concepts.name: Representation of the People Act, 1951: Disqualification on Conviction
key_dimensions: Section 8: Conviction for specific offences (moral turpitude, corruption, sedition etc.) with 2+ years imprisonment — disqualified for 6 years after release
Lily Thomas case (2013): SC struck down Section 8(4) which allowed sitting MPs/MLAs to escape immediate disqualification pending appeal — UPSC landmark ruling
Section 8A: Disqualification for corrupt practices as found by High Court in election petitions
UPSC trap: Disqualification under RPA is different from Art. 102 — Parliament cannot by law override SC's Lily Thomas ruling

concepts.name: Disqualification vs. Vacation of Seat: Conceptual Distinction
key_dimensions: Vacation (Art. 101): Seat becomes vacant due to dual membership, resignation, absence, etc. — no stigma attached
Disqualification (Art. 102): Member becomes ineligible — carries legal consequence and affects future candidacy
UPSC trap: Resignation from House ≠ disqualification; a resigned member can immediately contest by-election
Disqualified member under Tenth Schedule — can they contest immediately? SC in Manipur Speaker case addressed this ambiguity

concepts.name: Disqualification and By-Election: Can a Disqualified MP Re-contest?
key_dimensions: No constitutional bar on a disqualified MP contesting a by-election immediately unless specifically barred by RPA or other law
Tenth Schedule disqualification — no explicit bar on re-contesting from another party immediately
UPSC trap: Anti-defection disqualification does not prevent re-election — Rahul Gandhi Surat conviction case illustrated political dimensions
RPA Section 8 conviction disqualification bars contesting for 6 years post-release — stricter than Tenth Schedule

concepts.name: 91st Constitutional Amendment Act, 2003: Impact on Anti-Defection
key_dimensions: Abolished split (1/3rd) provision — only merger (2/3rd) exemption survives
Capped Council of Ministers at 15% of Lok Sabha/State Legislature strength — connected reform
UPSC trap: 91st Amendment also added that a member disqualified under Tenth Schedule cannot be appointed as a Minister until re-elected
Rationale: Prevent defection-induced governments and floor-crossing culture

concepts.name: Nominated Members and Anti-Defection Law
key_dimensions: Nominated members (Rajya Sabha under Art. 80, Anglo-Indian in original constitution) — special rule under Tenth Schedule
UPSC trap: Nominated member can join a political party within 6 months of taking oath — after 6 months, joining any party triggers disqualification
Anglo-Indian nominated provision abolished by 104th Amendment, 2020 — impacts Tenth Schedule application
Distinction: Nominated vs. elected members — different timeline for party joining

concepts.name: Independent MPs and Anti-Defection Law
key_dimensions: Independent MP who contests and wins without party affiliation — joining any political party after election leads to disqualification
UPSC trap: Independent MP has NO grace period unlike nominated member — immediate disqualification on joining party post-election
Rationale: Voter mandate was for an independent candidate; party allegiance changes voter's choice
Distinction: Independent MP can support any party from outside without disqualification — voting support ≠ membership

concepts.name: Governor's Role in State Legislature Disqualification vs. President's Role: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: Art. 192 (State) mirrors Art. 103 (Parliament) — Governor refers to EC, bound by EC's opinion
UPSC trap: For Tenth Schedule (anti-defection), it is the Speaker of Assembly/Chairman of Council — NOT the Governor
Governor has no role in anti-defection disqualifications — common UPSC confusion point
Symmetry between Union and State provisions — same EC consultation requirement

concepts.name: Disqualification Under Article 191 Read With Tenth Schedule: Specific to State Legislatures
key_dimensions: Art. 191 = State Legislature equivalent of Art. 102 for Parliament — UPSC tests this parallel constantly
Tenth Schedule applies to BOTH Parliament and State Legislatures — single schedule, unified law
Speaker of Vidhan Sabha/Chairman of Vidhan Parishad is the deciding authority — parallel to Lok Sabha Speaker/RS Chairman
Recent Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra political crises — practical application of Tenth Schedule in states

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Speaker's Disqualification Decision: Scope and Limits
key_dimensions: Kihoto Hollohan (1992): Judicial review available but limited — not at interlocutory stage, only after final order
Nabam Rebia case (2016): Speaker facing removal motion cannot decide disqualification petitions — conflict of interest
UPSC trap: Courts cannot review Speaker's decision on merits de novo — only on constitutional grounds (malafides, natural justice violation, perversity)
Tension between parliamentary privilege (Art. 105/194) and judicial oversight — ongoing constitutional debate

concepts.name: Election Commission's Advisory Role in Disqualification: Powers and Binding Nature
key_dimensions: EC's opinion is binding on President/Governor — not merely advisory (judicially interpreted post-ECI's own assertion)
EC conducts quasi-judicial proceedings before giving opinion — notices, hearings, evidence
UPSC trap: EC's role is ONLY for Art. 102(1)(a) to (d) grounds — NOT for Tenth Schedule anti-defection cases
EC also decides disputes between rival factions of a political party (symbol disputes) — related but distinct power

concepts.name: Disqualification and the Doctrine of 'Whip': Scope of Party Direction
key_dimensions: Tenth Schedule disqualification triggered by voting against or abstaining contrary to party whip — three-line whip is most binding
UPSC trap: Not every vote against party position triggers disqualification — only when 'whip' is specifically issued and disobeyed
Party can condone the defection within 15 days — if condoned, disqualification does not apply (UPSC tests this exception)
Free vote allowed by party = no disqualification even if member votes differently — party's explicit permission negates disqualification
